content: The Hungarian Oak, also known as the Italian Oak (Quercus frainetto; syn. Quercus farnetto Ten.), is a species of oak tree native to southeastern Europe, including parts of Italy, the Balkans, Hungary, Romania, and Turkey. It belongs to the Quercus sect. Mesobalanus. This is a large deciduous tree that can grow up to 38 meters in height, with a trunk diameter reaching nearly 2 meters. The leaves of the Hungarian Oak are notably large, measuring between 14 and 25 cm in length, though they can occasionally grow up to 33 cm. Their shape is variable, with 6 to 10 deeply incised parallel lobes, which are often further divided into sublobes. The leaf stalks are generally short, ranging from 2 to 6 mm in length, though they can occasionally extend up to 22 mm. The leaves are widest near the apex, which is broad and short-pointed. At the base, the leaves often feature ear-shaped projections (auricles) that may overlap the twig. When the leaves first expand, they are light yellow-green in color, but they darken to a rich green by early summer. The lower surface of the leaves is covered with fine russet hairs, and the leaves are typically clustered at the ends of the twigs. In autumn, the leaves turn shades of brown, russet, or yellow, and some may remain attached to the twigs until the following spring. The buds of the Hungarian Oak are large, elongated, and pointed, with a shiny russet or light brown color and a fine covering of minute hairs (tomentum). The twigs are stout and bear russet-colored, upward-pointing hairs. The acorns of this tree mature in approximately six months. They are light brown, egg-shaped, and typically measure 15 to 35 mm in length, with a blunt apex. The acorn cups are covered with long, overlapping scales and russet hairs. Acorns are usually found in clusters of two to eight at the ends of the twigs. The Hungarian Oak is primarily found in the Balkans, which is the center of its native range. It is well-adapted to the subcontinental climate of southeastern Europe, but its distribution is heavily influenced by soil conditions. This species thrives in heavy, acidic soils such as cambisols and vertisols, which are common in Serbia, Bulgaria, and Romania. These soils are often leached, very dry in summer, and occasionally waterlogged in spring. However, the Hungarian Oak does not tolerate flooding or high water tables and is highly sensitive to the presence of lime in the soil. As a result, despite its name, the Hungarian Oak is a rare tree in Hungary, where soils are typically rich in lime. The most widespread forest association of the Hungarian Oak in the Balkans is the Hungarian Oak-Turkey Oak forest (Quercetum frainetto-cerris Rud.), which is also the most common forest type in Serbia. In cultivation, the Hungarian Oak is considered an excellent ornamental tree, particularly suited for large gardens.
